'''Manolis Kellis''' ({{langx|el|Μανώλης Καμβυσέλλης}}; born 1977) is a professor of [[Computer science|Computer Science]] and [[Computational Biology]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)]] and a member of the [[Broad Institute]] of [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] and [[Harvard]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.csail.mit.edu/person/manolis-kellis|title=Manolis Kellis {{!}} MIT CSAIL|website=www.csail.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> He is the head of the Computational Biology Group at MIT<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://kellislab.com/lab-head|title=MIT Computational Biology Group|website=MIT Computational Biology Group Lab Head|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> and is a Principal Investigator in the [[MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory|Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab]] (CSAIL) at MIT.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.csail.mit.edu/person/manolis-kellis|title=People {{!}} MIT CSAIL|last=Kellis|first=Manolis|website=www.csail.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref>

Kellis is known for his contributions to [[genomics]], [[human genetics]], [[epigenomics]], [[Regulation of gene expression|gene regulation]], [[genome evolution]], [[Genome-wide association study|disease mechanism]], and [[Single cell genomics|single-cell genomics]]. He co-led the [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] Roadmap Epigenomics Project<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.roadmapepigenomics.org/|title=Roadmap Epigenomics Project - Home|website=www.roadmapepigenomics.org|access-date=2018-07-24|archive-date=2021-04-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408031928/http://www.roadmapepigenomics.org/}}</ref> effort to == Education and early career ==

Kellis was born in Greece, moved with his family to France when he was 12, and came to the U.S. in 1993.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.mit.edu/2012/profile-kellis-0417|title=Getting to the root of genetics|work=MIT News|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> He obtained his [[B.S.]], [[M.Eng.]], and [[Ph.D.]] from MIT, where he worked with [[Eric Lander]], founding director of the Broad Institute, and [[Bonnie Berger]], professor at MIT<ref name=":13" /> and received the Sprowls award for the best doctorate thesis in Computer Science,<ref name=":12" /> and the first Paris Kanellakis graduate fellowship.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eecs.mit.edu/academics-admissions/graduate-program/eecs-graduate-student-fellowship-awards-news/kanellakis|title=Kanellakis Fellowships {{!}} MIT EECS|website=www.eecs.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19|archive-date=2014-08-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808131013/http://www.eecs.mit.edu/academics-admissions/graduate-program/eecs-graduate-student-fellowship-awards-news/kanellakis}}</ref> Prior to computational biology, he worked on artificial intelligence, sketch and image recognition, robotics, and computational geometry, at MIT and at the [[Xerox Palo Alto Research Center]].<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|url=https://www.genome.gov/pages/about/nachgr/2004nachgragenda/tabekelliscv.pdf|title=Manolis Kellis MIT Center for Genome Research Resume|access-date=2018-07-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180822114741/https://www.genome.gov/pages/about/nachgr/2004nachgragenda/tabekelliscv.pdf|archive-date=2018-08-22}}</ref>

=== Comparative genomics ===
Kellis started comparing the genomes of yeast species as an MIT graduate student. As part of this work, which was published in ''Nature'' in 2003,<ref name=":14" /> he developed computational methods to pinpoint patterns of similarity and difference between closely related genomes. The goal was to develop methods for understanding genomes with a view to apply them to the human genome.

He turned from yeast to flies and ultimately to mammals, comparing multiple species to explore genes, their control elements, and their deregulation in human disease.<ref name=":8" />  Kellis led several comparative genomics projects in human,<ref name=":8">{{Cite news|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/601544/reinterpreting-the-human-genome/|title=Annotating the book of life|last=Schaffer|first=Amanda|work=MIT Technology Review|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> mammals,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xie|first1=Xiaohui|last2=Lu|first2=Jun|last3=Kulbokas|first3=E. J.|last4=Golub|first4=Todd R.|last5=Mootha|first5=Vamsi|last6=Lindblad-Toh|first6=Kerstin|last7=Lander|first7=Eric S.|last8=Kellis|first8=Manolis|date=2005-02-27|title=Systematic discovery of regulatory motifs in human promoters and 3′ UTRs by comparison of several mammals|journal=Nature|volume=434|issue=7031|pages=338–345|doi=10.1038/nature03441|pmid=15735639|pmc=2923337|bibcode=2005Natur.434..338X|issn=0028-0836}}</ref><ref name="Lindblad-Toh 2011 476–482"/> flies,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lin|first1=Michael F.|last2=Carlson|first2=Joseph W.|last3=Crosby|first3=Madeline A.|last4=Matthews|first4=Beverley B.|last5=Yu|first5=Charles|last6=Park|first6=Soo|last7=Wan|first7=Kenneth H.|last8=Schroeder|first8=Andrew J.|last9=Kellis|first9=Manolis|date=2007|title=Revisiting the protein-coding gene catalog of Drosophila melanogaster using 12 fly genomes|pmid=17989253|journal=Genome Research|volume=17|issue=12|pages=1823–1836|doi=10.1101/gr.6679507|issn=1088-9051|pmc=2099591}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stark|first1=Alexander|last2=Lin|first2=Michael F.|last3=Kheradpour|first3=Pouya|last4=Pedersen|first4=Jakob S.|last5=Parts|first5=Leopold|last6=Carlson|first6=Joseph W.|last7=Crosby|first7=Madeline A.|last8=Rasmussen|first8=Matthew D.|last9=Kellis|first9=Manolis|date=2007|title=Discovery of functional elements in 12 Drosophila genomes using evolutionary signatures|journal=Nature|volume=450|issue=7167|pages=219–232|doi=10.1038/nature06340|pmid=17994088|pmc=2474711|bibcode=2007Natur.450..219S|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> and yeast.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kellis|first1=Manolis|last2=Birren|first2=Bruce W.|last3=Lander|first3=Eric S.|date=2004-03-07|title=Proof and evolutionary analysis of ancient genome duplication in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae|journal=Nature|volume=428|issue=6983|pages=617–624|doi=10.1038/nature02424|pmid=15004568|bibcode=2004Natur.428..617K|s2cid=4422074|issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

=== Epigenomics ===
Kellis co-led the NIH government-funded project to catalogue the human epigenome. He said during an interview with [[MIT Technology Review]]<ref name=":8" /> "If the genome is the book of life, the epigenome is the complete set of annotations and bookmarks."<ref name=":8" /> His lab now uses this map to further the understanding of fundamental processes and disease in humans.

=== Obesity ===
Kellis and colleagues used epigenomic data to investigate the mechanistic basis of the strongest genetic association with obesity, published in the [[The New England Journal of Medicine|New England Journal of Medicine]].<ref name=":3" /> They showed that this mechanism operates in the fat cells of both humans and mice and detailed how changes within the relevant genomic regions cause a shift from dissipating energy as heat ([[thermogenesis]]) to storing energy as fat.<ref name=":5" /> A full understanding of the phenomenon may lead to treatments for people whose 'slow metabolism' cause them to gain excessive weight.<ref name=":4" />

=== Alzheimer's disease ===
Kellis, [[Li-Huei Tsai]], and others at MIT used epigenomic markings in human and mouse brains to study the mechanisms leading to [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer]]'s disease, published in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] in 2015.<ref name=":6" /> They showed that immune cell activation and inflammation, which have long been associated with the condition, are not simply the result of neurodegeneration, as some researchers have argued. Rather, in mice engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like symptoms, they found that immune cells start to change even before neural changes are observed.<ref name=":7" />

=== Single-cell Genomics ===
The Kellis Lab has profiled a large number of human post-mortem brains at [[Single-cell transcriptomics|single-cell]] resolution, studying inter-individual variation associated with genetic differences and disease phenotypes, including the first [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1195-2 single-cell transcriptomic analysis of Alzheimer's disease] (Nature, 2019).

=== Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) ===
Kellis is a member of the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project that seeks to elucidate the basis of disease predisposition. It is an NIH-sponsored project that seeks to characterize genetic variation in human tissues with roles in diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.<ref name=":2" />

Kellis is also a Principal Investigator of the enhancing GTEx (eGTEx) consortium, studying [[Epigenetics|epigenomic]] changes of regulatory elements and [[Epitranscriptomic sequencing|epitranscriptomic]] changes of RNA transcripts across multiple human tissues.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Xiong |first1=Xushen |last2=Hou |first2=Lei |last3=Park |first3=Yongjin P. |last4=Molinie |first4=Benoit |last5=Gregory |first5=Richard I. |last6=Kellis |first6=Manolis |date=August 2021 |title=Genetic drivers of m6A methylation in human brain, lung, heart and muscle |journal=Nature Genetics |language=en |volume=53 |issue=8 |pages=1156–1165 |doi=10.1038/s41588-021-00890-3 |pmid=34211177 |pmc=9112289 |issn=1546-1718}}</ref>

=== Teaching ===

In addition to his research, Kellis co-taught for several years MIT's required undergraduate introductory [[algorithm]] courses 6.006: Introduction to Algorithms and 6.046: Design and Analysis of Algorithms<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.006/spring11/staff.shtml|title=6.006: Introduction to Algorithms - Massachusetts Institute of Technology|website=courses.csail.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://stellar.mit.edu/S/course/6/sp06/6.046/|title=6.046/18.410 Class Home|website=stellar.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-20}}</ref> with Profs. [[Ron Rivest]], [[Erik Demaine]], [[Piotr Indyk]], Srinivas Devadas and others.

He is also teaching a [[computational biology]] course at MIT, titled "Computational Biology: Genomes, Networks, Evolution."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://stellar.mit.edu/S/course/6/fa17/6.047/|title=6.047/6.878 Class Home|website=stellar.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> The course (6.047/6.878) is geared towards advanced undergraduate and early graduate students, seeking to learn the algorithmic and machine learning foundations of computational biology, and also be exposed to current frontiers of research in order to become active practitioners of the field.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/electrical-engineering-and-computer-science/6-047-computational-biology-fall-2015/|title=Computational Biology|website=MIT OpenCourseWare|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> He started 6.881: [https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-881-computational-personal-genomics-making-sense-of-complete-genomes-spring-2016/ Computational Personal Genomics: Making sense of complete genomes], and 6.883/9.S99: [https://twitter.com/manoliskellis/status/1486105467839418371 Neurogenomics: Computational Molecular Neuroscience] This course is aimed at exploring the computational challenges associated with interpreting how sequence differences between individuals lead to phenotypic differences such as gene expression, disease predisposition, or response to treatment.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/electrical-engineering-and-computer-science/6-881-computational-personal-genomics-making-sense-of-complete-genomes-spring-2016/|title=Computational Personal Genomics: Making Sense of Complete Genomes|website=MIT OpenCourseWare|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref>

=== Awards and honors===

Kellis received the US [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]] (PECASE),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eecs.mit.edu/news-events/media/aaronson-kellis-recipients-pecase-2010-award|title=Aaronson, Kellis recipients of PECASE 2010 Award {{!}} MIT EECS|website=www.eecs.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> the [[National Science Foundation CAREER Awards|National Science Foundation CAREER award]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=0644282|title=NSF Award Search: Award#0644282 - CAREER: Comparative Genomics and Biological Signal Discovery in the Human Genome|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sloan.org/past-fellows|title=Sloan Foundation Fellows|website=sloan.org|access-date=2018-07-19|archive-date=2018-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314000756/https://sloan.org/past-fellows}}</ref> the [[Gregor Mendel]] Medal for Outstanding Achievements in Science by the [[Mendel Lectures]] committee, the Athens Information Technology (AIT) Niki Award for Science and Engineering,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.csail.mit.edu/news/kellis-wins-niki-award|title=Kellis Wins Niki Award {{!}} MIT CSAIL|website=www.csail.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> the Ruth and Joel Spira Teaching award,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://engineering.mit.edu/faculty-research/faculty-awards/teaching-awards/|title=MIT School of Engineering {{!}} » Teaching Awards|work=Mit Engineering|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> and the George M. Sprowls Award for the best Ph.D. thesis in Computer Science at MIT.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|url=http://akron.csail.mit.edu/csailawards/year/desc/all|title=All Awards {{!}} MIT CSAIL|website=csail.mit.edu|access-date=2018-07-19}}</ref> He was named as one of Technology Review's Top 35 Innovators Under 35 for his research in comparative genomics<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?TRID=467|title=Innovator Under 35: Manolis Kellis, 29|last=MIT Technology Review|website=MIT Technology Review|access-date=2018-07-19|archive-date=2018-07-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180727235118/http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?trid=467}}</ref>
